# Maya

## Canonical Name

Maya

## Sanskrit

माया

## Transliteration

Māyā

## Śabda

माया

## Dhātu

मा (Mā) — To measure, to create, to construct. Māyā is "that which measures out" or "that which creates the appearance of measure and form."

## Vyākaraṇa

Māyā is a feminine noun. Derived from the root mā (to measure/create) with the suffix -yā. In Vedic usage, māyā means "supernatural power" or "creative magic." In Advaita Vedānta, it acquires the technical meaning of "cosmic illusion."

## Nirukta

"Māyate iti māyā" — that which measures/creates. Also: "mā — not, yā — that which is" — that which is not (the appearance of what is not real). The second etymology is a later philosophical interpretation.

## Bīja

ह्रीं (Hrīm) — the bīja of Māyā-Śakti in Tantric traditions. Hrīm is the bīja of the Goddess as the creative power of illusion and liberation.

## Tattva

Māyā-Tattva — the principle of creative illusion and cosmic appearance. In Advaita: Māyā is the power of Brahman that projects the apparent multiplicity of the universe. In Kashmir Śaivism: Māyā is one of the five kañcukas (coverings) that limit the universal consciousness.

## Śakti

Māyā-Śakti — the creative and concealing power. Māyā has two functions: āvaraṇa-śakti (concealing power — it conceals Brahman) and vikṣepa-śakti (projecting power — it projects the apparent world).

## Literal Meaning

Illusion; creative power; supernatural power; the cosmic appearance.

## Functional Meaning

Māyā is the cosmic power that creates the appearance of multiplicity in the non-dual Brahman. It is neither real (sat) nor unreal (asat) — it is anirvachanīya (indescribable). Māyā operates through avidyā (ignorance) at the individual level and through the cosmic creative power at the universal level. Liberation (mokṣa) is the transcendence of māyā through jñāna (knowledge).

## Ontology

In Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Māyā is the power of Brahman that creates the appearance of the world. It is neither real nor unreal — it is mithyā (apparent). The world is not non-existent (it appears) but not ultimately real (it is not Brahman). In Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Māyā is Viṣṇu's creative power — real, not illusory. In Dvaita (Madhva): Māyā is Viṣṇu's power — the world created by māyā is real. In Kashmir Śaivism: Māyā is one of the thirty-six tattvas — a real power of Śiva that limits universal consciousness.

## Cosmology

In Purāṇic cosmology: Māyā is Viṣṇu's creative power (Yoga-Māyā) that maintains the cosmic illusion. The Devī Māhātmya describes Māyā as the Goddess herself — the cosmic creative power. In Sāṃkhya: Prakṛti (primal matter) is the equivalent of Māyā — the creative power that produces the universe for Puruṣa's experience.

## Psychology

Māyā as psychological principle: avidyā (individual ignorance) is the psychological form of cosmic māyā. The three psychological functions of māyā: āvaraṇa (concealment of the true Self), vikṣepa (projection of the false self), and mala (impurity). Liberation requires the removal of māyā through viveka (discrimination) and vairāgya (dispassion).

## Governance

The concept of māyā in governance: the ruler who is deluded by māyā governs for personal gain rather than dharma. The Arthaśāstra warns against the māyā of power — the illusion that the king is the ultimate authority. The concept of rāja-māyā (royal illusion) — the danger of rulers believing their own propaganda.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: māyā (illusion/delusion) is a cause of mental disease (mānasa-roga). The concept of prajñāparādha (crime against wisdom) — acting against one's better knowledge — is the Āyurvedic equivalent of māyā's concealing function.

## Mathematics

The concept of māyā in mathematics: the appearance of multiplicity from unity mirrors the mathematical concept of differentiation. The concept of māyā as "measurement" (from the root mā) connects to the mathematical act of measuring — imposing finite measure on the infinite.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Māyā is associated with the Moon (Candra) — the planet of illusion, reflection, and the mind. The Moon's phases represent māyā's changing appearances. The concept of graha-māyā (planetary illusion) — the apparent retrograde motion of planets is a form of māyā.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: māyā is the appearance of base metals as gold — the alchemist's task is to see through māyā to the true nature of substances. The concept of māyā in metallurgy: the surface appearance of a metal (its color, luster) may conceal its true nature.

## Ritual

The concept of māyā in ritual: ritual itself operates within māyā — it uses the apparent world to point beyond it. The concept of māyā-pūjā (worship through the apparent) — using forms, images, and rituals to transcend form. The Tantric tradition explicitly works with māyā — using the apparent world as the path to liberation.

## Symbolism

The veil symbolizes māyā — it conceals what is behind it. The mirror symbolizes māyā — it creates an apparent reflection that is not the original. The dream symbolizes māyā — vivid and real while experienced, but recognized as unreal upon waking. The magician (māyāvī) symbolizes māyā's creative power.

## Related Deities

- Devī/Mahāmāyā (the Goddess as the cosmic māyā-power)
- Viṣṇu (Yoga-Māyā — his creative power)
- Śiva (Māyā as his śakti)
- Durgā (the Goddess who wields māyā to protect dharma)

## Related Lokas

- All lokas are within māyā — they are māyā's projections
- Brahmaloka is beyond māyā

## Related Koshas

- All five koshas are māyā's projections
- Ānandamaya Kosha is the subtlest form of māyā

## Related Chakras

- Ājñā (third eye) — the chakra of discrimination that sees through māyā
- Sahasrāra (crown) — beyond māyā

## Related Yantras

- Śrī Yantra (the geometric form of Māyā-Śakti's creative power)
- Hrīm Yantra (the yantra of Māyā-bīja)

## Related Mantras

- "Hrīm" (the bīja of Māyā-Śakti)
- "Om aim hrīm klīm cāmuṇḍāyai vicce" (Navārṇa Mantra — invoking the Goddess beyond māyā)

## Related Vidyās

- Māyā Vidyā (the science of cosmic illusion — Advaita Vedānta)
- Śakti Vidyā (the science of the Goddess as māyā-power)

## Related Śāstras

- Māṇḍūkya Kārikā (Gauḍapāda — māyā as the basis of the apparent world)
- Vivekacūḍāmaṇi (Śaṅkara — māyā and its transcendence)
- Devī Māhātmya (Māyā as the Goddess)
- Yoga Vāsiṣṭha (māyā and liberation)

## Traditional Interpretations

- Advaita Vedānta: Māyā is the cosmic illusion — neither real nor unreal; transcended by jñāna
- Viśiṣṭādvaita: Māyā is Viṣṇu's real creative power — the world is real
- Dvaita: Māyā is Viṣṇu's power — the world created by māyā is real
- Śākta: Māyā is the Goddess herself — the creative power of the universe
- Kashmir Śaivism: Māyā is one of the thirty-six tattvas — a real power of Śiva

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Māyā as supernatural creative power (of Varuṇa, Indra)
- Upaniṣadic period: Māyā as the creative power of Brahman
- Gauḍapāda (7th century CE): Māyā as the basis of the apparent world
- Śaṅkara (8th century CE): Māyā as cosmic illusion — the central concept of Advaita
- Rāmānuja (11th century CE): Critique of Śaṅkara's māyā — the world is real
- Modern: Māyā as a concept in comparative philosophy and consciousness studies

## Cross References

- Brahman
- Avidya (ignorance — individual māyā)
- Prakrti (Sāṃkhya equivalent)
- Shakti
- Moksha (liberation from māyā)

## Open Research Questions

- Is Śaṅkara's concept of māyā coherent? Can something be "neither real nor unreal"?
- How does the Advaita concept of māyā relate to the Buddhist concept of śūnyatā (emptiness)?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some philosophers of mind propose that the Advaita concept of māyā anticipates the modern philosophical problem of the "veil of perception" — the question of whether we perceive reality directly or only its appearances. This remains a philosophical analogy.

## Canonical Sources

- Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10 (māyā as the Goddess's creative power)
- Māṇḍūkya Kārikā (Gauḍapāda)
- Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya (Śaṅkara)
- Devī Māhātmya 1.55-56 (Mahāmāyā)
- Bhagavad Gītā 7.14 (daivī māyā — divine illusion)

- Sahasrāra (crown) — beyond māyā

## Related Yantras

- Śrī Yantra (the geometric form of Māyā-Śakti's creative power)
- Hrīm Yantra (the yantra of Māyā-bīja)

- "Hrīm" (the bīja of Māyā-Śakti)
- "Om aim hrīm klīm cāmuṇḍāyai vicce" (Navārṇa Mantra — invoking the Goddess beyond māyā)

- Māyā Vidyā (the science of cosmic illusion — Advaita Vedānta)
- Śakti Vidyā (the science of the Goddess as māyā-power)

## Related Śāstras

- Māṇḍūkya Kārikā (Gauḍapāda — māyā as the basis of the apparent world)
- Vivekacūḍāmaṇi (Śaṅkara — māyā and its transcendence)
- Devī Māhātmya (Māyā as the Goddess)

- Viśiṣṭādvaita: Māyā is Viṣṇu's real creative power — the world is real
- Dvaita: Māyā is Viṣṇu's power — the world created by māyā is real
- Śākta: Māyā is the Goddess herself — the creative power of the universe
- Kashmir Śaivism: Māyā is one of the thirty-six tattvas — a real power of Śiva

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Māyā as supernatural creative power (of Varuṇa, Indra)
- Upaniṣadic period: Māyā as the creative power of Brahman
- Gauḍapāda (7th century CE): Māyā as the basis of the apparent world
- Śaṅkara (8th century CE): Māyā as cosmic illusion — the central concept of Advaita
- Rāmānuja (11th century CE): Critique of Śaṅkara's māyā — the world is real

# Brahman

## Canonical Name

Brahman

## Sanskrit

ब्रह्मन्

## Transliteration

Brahman

## Śabda

ब्रह्मन्

## Dhātu

बृह् (Bṛh) — To expand, to grow, to be great.

## Vyākaraṇa

Brahman is a neuter noun (not to be confused with Brahmā, the masculine creator deity, or Brāhmaṇa, the priestly class). Derived from the root bṛh with the suffix -man. The neuter gender indicates that Brahman transcends all categories including gender.

## Nirukta

Yāska: "bṛhati iti brahma" — that which is great, that which expands. Brahman is the infinitely expanding reality that underlies all existence.

## Bīja

ॐ (Om/Auṃ) — the primordial sound that is the sonic form of Brahman. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad opens: "Auṃ ity etad akṣaram idaṃ sarvam" — Om, this syllable is all this.

## Tattva

Brahma-Tattva — the principle of absolute, infinite, self-luminous reality. Brahman is described as Sat-Cit-Ānanda (Being-Consciousness-Bliss) — not three qualities but three aspects of one indivisible reality.

## Śakti

Brahman's śakti is Māyā — the creative power that projects the apparent multiplicity of the universe. In Śākta traditions, Brahman without Śakti is inert (śava); Brahman with Śakti is Śiva (the living absolute).

## Literal Meaning

The Absolute; the Infinite; the Ultimate Reality; the Ground of Being.

## Functional Meaning

Brahman is the infinite, eternal, unchanging absolute reality that is the ground of all existence. It is both the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) and the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa) of the universe. Brahman is described via two approaches: Nirguṇa Brahman (without attributes — the absolute beyond all description) and Saguṇa Brahman (with attributes — the personal God, Īśvara). The Upaniṣads teach that Brahman is identical with Ātman (the individual Self).

## Ontology

In Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Brahman alone is real (Brahma satyam); the world is appearance (jagat mithyā); the individual self is Brahman (jīvo brahmaiva nāparaḥ). In Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Brahman is real, personal (Viṣṇu), and the universe and souls are Brahman's body. In Dvaita (Madhva): Brahman (Viṣṇu) is real and eternally distinct from souls and world. In Śaiva Siddhānta: Brahman is Śiva, the supreme reality with infinite śaktis.

## Cosmology

Brahman is the source, sustainer, and dissolution point of all universes. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad: "yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante" — from which all beings are born, by which they live, into which they return — that is Brahman. The Purāṇas describe Brahman as the ocean from which the universe arises like waves. The concept of Brahmaṇḍa (Brahman's egg) is the cosmic egg from which the universe hatches.

## Psychology

Brahman as psychological reality: the deepest layer of consciousness is Brahman. In Yoga psychology, the state of samādhi (absorption) is the direct experience of Brahman. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad identifies Brahman with the fourth state of consciousness (turīya) that underlies waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. The experience of Brahman is described as "neti neti" (not this, not this) — Brahman cannot be grasped by the mind but is the ground of the mind.

## Governance

The concept of Brahman in governance: the ideal ruler is one who has realized Brahman and governs from that realization. The Arthaśāstra's concept of the philosopher-king parallels the Upaniṣadic ideal of the Brahman-realized ruler. The concept of Brahma-rāṣṭra (the kingdom of Brahman) appears in Vedic literature as the ideal polity.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Brahman is the ultimate source of health (ārogya). The concept of Brahma-cakra (the cycle of Brahman) underlies the Āyurvedic understanding of the body as a microcosm of the universe. The highest healing is Brahma-jñāna (knowledge of Brahman) which removes the root cause of all disease — avidyā (ignorance).

## Mathematics

The concept of Brahman in mathematics: Brahman as the infinite (ananta) is the philosophical basis for the Indian mathematical concept of infinity. The concept of śūnya (zero) as the void from which all numbers emerge mirrors the Brahman-as-source concept. The Upaniṣadic statement "pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam" (that is full, this is full) is a mathematical statement about the nature of infinity.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Brahman is identified with the cosmic space (ākāśa) in which all celestial bodies move. The concept of Brahma-muhūrta (the hour of Brahman — 1.5 hours before sunrise) is the most auspicious time for spiritual practice. The Milky Way (Ākāśagaṅgā) is considered the visible form of Brahman's cosmic body.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: Brahman is the philosophical gold (parama-suvarṇa) — the ultimate substance that all metals aspire to become. The alchemical process of transmutation mirrors the spiritual process of realizing Brahman beneath the apparent multiplicity of substances.

## Ritual

The Brahma-yajña (sacrifice to Brahman) is the daily recitation of the Vedas — the highest ritual act. The Upanayana ceremony initiates the student into the study of Brahman. The Mahāvākyas are transmitted in ritual contexts as the direct teaching of Brahman. The concept of Brahma-vidyā (knowledge of Brahman) is the ultimate goal of all Vedic ritual.

## Symbolism

Om (ॐ) is the primary symbol of Brahman — the sound of the universe. The infinite space (ākāśa) symbolizes Brahman's all-pervading nature. The ocean symbolizes Brahman — waves (individual beings) arise from and return to the ocean. The sun symbolizes Nirguṇa Brahman — self-luminous, the source of all light. The bindu (point) in the center of a yantra represents Brahman as the source of all manifestation.

## Related Deities

- Brahman is not a deity but the ground of all deities
- Brahma (the creator) is Saguṇa Brahman's creative aspect
- Viṣṇu (the preserver) is Saguṇa Brahman's sustaining aspect
- Śiva (the destroyer) is Saguṇa Brahman's dissolving aspect
- Devī (the Goddess) is Brahman's Śakti — the dynamic aspect of the absolute

## Related Lokas

- Brahmaloka (Satyaloka) — the highest realm, closest to Brahman
- All lokas are within Brahman — "sarvam khalv idaṃ brahma" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1)

## Related Koshas

- All five koshas are within Brahman
- Ānandamaya Kosha (bliss sheath) is the closest approximation to Brahman in the individual
- Beyond all koshas is Ātman = Brahman

## Related Chakras

- Sahasrāra (crown chakra) — the seat of Brahman realization in the individual body
- The entire chakra system is within Brahman

## Related Yantras

- Śrī Yantra (the geometric representation of Brahman's creative expansion)
- Bindu (the central point — Brahman as the source)

## Related Mantras

- "Aum" (the sonic form of Brahman)
- "Aham Brahmāsmi" (I am Brahman — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10)
- "Prajñānam Brahma" (Consciousness is Brahman — Aitareya Upaniṣad 3.3)
- "Sarvam khalv idaṃ brahma" (All this is indeed Brahman — Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1)

## Related Vidyās

- Brahmavidyā (knowledge of Brahman — the supreme vidyā)
- Ātmavidyā (self-knowledge = Brahmavidyā)
- Upaniṣad Vidyā (the teaching of the Upaniṣads)

## Related Śāstras

- Upaniṣads (primary source — especially Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Chāndogya, Taittirīya, Māṇḍūkya)
- Brahma Sūtras (Bādarāyaṇa — systematic exposition of Brahman)
- Bhagavad Gītā (Chapter 13 — Kṣetra-Kṣetrajña; Chapter 14 — Guṇatraya Vibhāga)
- Vivekacūḍāmaṇi (Śaṅkara)
- Brahma-Sūtra-Bhāṣya (Śaṅkara's commentary)

## Traditional Interpretations

- Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Brahman alone is real; world and individual self are appearances in Brahman
- Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Brahman is personal (Viṣṇu); world and souls are Brahman's body
- Dvaita (Madhva): Brahman (Viṣṇu) is real and eternally distinct from souls and world
- Śaiva Siddhānta: Brahman is Śiva with infinite śaktis
- Śākta: Brahman is the Goddess (Devī) — the dynamic absolute
- Kashmir Śaivism: Brahman is Śiva-Śakti — pure consciousness and its creative power

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Brahman primarily means "sacred utterance" or "prayer power"
- Atharvaveda: Brahman as cosmic power
- Brāhmaṇa period: Brahman as the power of ritual
- Early Upaniṣads: Brahman as the ultimate reality, identical with Ātman
- Brahma Sūtras (200 BCE–200 CE): Systematic philosophy of Brahman
- Śaṅkara (8th century CE): Advaita — Brahman as the only reality
- Rāmānuja (11th century CE): Viśiṣṭādvaita — Brahman as personal God
- Madhva (13th century CE): Dvaita — Brahman as Viṣṇu, eternally distinct

## Cross References

- Atman
- Moksha
- Maya
- Ishvara (personal God as Saguṇa Brahman)
- Purusha
- Om

## Open Research Questions

- Is Nirguṇa Brahman (attributeless absolute) a coherent philosophical concept, or does it collapse into nothingness?
- How does the Advaita concept of Brahman relate to the Buddhist concept of śūnyatā (emptiness)?
- What is the relationship between Brahman and the modern cosmological concept of the quantum vacuum?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some physicists and philosophers propose that the quantum vacuum (the ground state of quantum field theory) has structural similarities to the Upaniṣadic concept of Brahman as the ground of all existence. This remains a philosophical analogy, not an established scientific or canonical claim.

## Canonical Sources

- Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1 (Brahman as the source of all)
- Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1 (Sarvam khalv idaṃ brahma)
- Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10 (Aham Brahmāsmi)
- Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad (Brahman as the four states of consciousness)
- Brahma Sūtras 1.1.1 (Athāto brahma-jijñāsā — now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman)

# Kala

## Canonical Name

Kala

## Sanskrit

काल

## Transliteration

Kāla

## Śabda

काल

## Dhātu

कल् (Kal) — To count, to calculate; also connected to कल् (Kal) — to drive, to impel. Time is that which counts/measures and that which drives all things forward.

## Vyākaraṇa

Kāla is a masculine noun. It has two distinct meanings: (1) time (the cosmic principle), (2) death/Yama (the lord of time). The same word means both "time" and "death" — time is the force that leads all things to death.

## Nirukta

"Kalayati iti kālaḥ" — that which counts/measures. Also: "kālayati sarvam iti kālaḥ" — that which drives everything forward. Time is the universal driver.

## Bīja

क्रीं (Krīm) — the bīja of Kālī (the Goddess of time and death). Also कं (Kaṃ) — the bīja of Brahmā (the creator who operates within time).

## Tattva

Kāla-Tattva — the principle of time. In Sāṃkhya: Kāla is not a separate tattva but the mode of Prakṛti's activity. In Kashmir Śaivism: Kāla is one of the five kañcukas (coverings) that limit the universal consciousness — it limits the soul's experience to a particular time.

## Śakti

Kāla-Śakti — the power of time. The śakti that drives all change and transformation. Kālī (the Goddess of time) is the personification of Kāla-Śakti.

## Literal Meaning

Time; the right time; death; the black one (Kāla = black = death).

## Functional Meaning

Kāla is the universal principle of time that governs all change, growth, decay, and death. It operates at multiple levels: Kṣaṇa (moment), Muhūrta (48 minutes), Ahorātra (day-night), Pakṣa (fortnight), Māsa (month), Ṛtu (season), Ayana (half-year), Saṃvatsara (year), Yuga (cosmic age), Kalpa (cosmic cycle). The Bhagavad Gītā (11.32) identifies Kāla with Kṛṣṇa himself: "Kālo'smi loka-kṣaya-kṛt pravṛddhaḥ" — I am time, the destroyer of worlds.

## Ontology

In Vaiśeṣika: Kāla is one of the nine dravyas (substances) — eternal, all-pervading, the cause of all temporal relations. In Sāṃkhya: Kāla is not a separate substance but the mode of Prakṛti's activity. In Advaita: Kāla is within māyā — from the absolute standpoint, there is no time. In Kashmir Śaivism: Kāla is one of the five kañcukas that limit the soul.

## Cosmology

In Vedic cosmology: the four yugas (Kṛta/Satya, Tretā, Dvāpara, Kali) constitute a mahāyuga (4,320,000 years). 1000 mahāyugas = one kalpa (day of Brahmā = 4.32 billion years). The concept of mahāpralaya (great dissolution) at the end of Brahmā's life (311 trillion years). The Purāṇas describe Kāla as the cosmic force that drives the universe through its cycles.

## Psychology

Kāla as psychological principle: the experience of time is subjective — time flies in joy and drags in suffering. The concept of kāla-jñāna (knowledge of time) — the wise person knows the right time for action. The concept of kāla-yoga (the yoga of time) — acting in alignment with the cosmic time.

## Governance

The concept of Kāla in governance: the Arthaśāstra emphasizes kāla (timing) as one of the most important factors in governance. The concept of kāla-nīti (time-policy) — the right action at the right time. The concept of kāla-cakra (wheel of time) in political philosophy — empires rise and fall according to the wheel of time.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Kāla (time) is one of the three causes of disease (along with karma and prajñāparādha). The concept of kāla-parīkṣā (examination of time) — the physician must consider the time of day, season, and stage of life in diagnosis and treatment. The concept of kāla-bala (strength of time) — certain times are more favorable for treatment.

## Mathematics

In Vedic mathematics: Kāla is the basis of the Indian number system — the large numbers (millions, billions, trillions) were developed to measure cosmic time. The concept of kāla-gaṇita (time calculation) — the mathematics of astronomical cycles.

## Astronomy

Jyotiṣa (Vedic astronomy) is fundamentally the science of Kāla — tracking the movements of celestial bodies to determine auspicious times. The concept of kāla-cakra (wheel of time) in Jyotiṣa — the zodiac as the wheel of cosmic time. The nakṣatra system, the tithi (lunar day), and the muhūrta (auspicious time) are all expressions of Kāla.

## Metallurgy

The concept of Kāla in metallurgy: the right time for metallurgical processes — certain times are more auspicious for smelting, forging, and casting. The concept of kāla-karma (time-action) in metallurgy.

## Ritual

The concept of Kāla in ritual: all Vedic rituals are performed at specific times determined by Jyotiṣa. The concept of muhūrta (auspicious time) — the right moment for ritual action. The concept of kāla-pūjā (worship of time) — the Kālī pūjā is the worship of the Goddess of time.

## Symbolism

The wheel (cakra) symbolizes Kāla — the wheel of time that turns without stopping. The serpent eating its own tail (Ouroboros) symbolizes the cyclical nature of time. The skull (kapāla) symbolizes Kāla as death. The hourglass symbolizes the finite nature of human time within infinite cosmic time.

## Related Deities

- Kālī (the Goddess of time and death — the personification of Kāla)
- Yama (Kāla — the lord of death and time)
- Śiva (Mahākāla — the great time, the lord of cosmic cycles)
- Kṛṣṇa (identifies himself as Kāla in the Bhagavad Gītā)

## Related Lokas

- Kālaloka (the realm of time — the realm of Yama)
- All lokas exist within Kāla

## Related Koshas

- All five koshas exist within Kāla — they are temporal
- Beyond all koshas is the Ātman — beyond time

## Related Chakras

- Mūlādhāra (root chakra) — the seat of temporal existence and survival
- Sahasrāra (crown chakra) — beyond time (kālātīta)

## Related Yantras

- Kālī Yantra (the yantra of the Goddess of time)
- Kāla Yantra (for working with time in ritual)

## Related Mantras

- "Kālo'smi loka-kṣaya-kṛt pravṛddhaḥ" (Bhagavad Gītā 11.32)
- Kālī Mantra: "Om krīm kālikāyai namaḥ"
- Mahākāla Mantra: "Om hrīm śrīm krīm paramēśvari svāhā"

## Related Vidyās

- Kāla Vidyā (the science of time — Jyotiṣa)
- Kālacakra Vidyā (the science of the wheel of time — Buddhist and Hindu)

## Related Śāstras

- Bhagavad Gītā 11.32 (Kṛṣṇa as Kāla)
- Vaiśeṣika Sūtras (Kāla as a substance)
- Arthaśāstra (Kāla in governance)
- Jyotiṣa texts (Kāla in astronomy)

## Traditional Interpretations

- Vaiśeṣika: Kāla is an eternal, all-pervading substance — the cause of all temporal relations
- Advaita: Kāla is within māyā — from the absolute standpoint, there is no time
- Kashmir Śaivism: Kāla is one of the five kañcukas that limit the soul
- Śākta: Kāla is the Goddess Kālī — the power of time and liberation

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Kāla as the cosmic time that governs the universe
- Upaniṣadic period: Kāla as the force that drives all beings to death
- Purāṇic period: Kāla as the cosmic cycles (yugas, kalpas)
- Bhagavad Gītā: Kāla as Kṛṣṇa himself — the destroyer of worlds
- Tantric period: Kāla as the Goddess Kālī — the liberating power of time

## Cross References

- Dharma
- Karma
- Maya
- Brahman (beyond time)
- Atman (beyond time)

## Open Research Questions

- What is the relationship between the Vedic concept of Kāla and modern physics' concept of time (spacetime, arrow of time)?
- How does the concept of kāla-cakra (wheel of time) relate to modern cosmological theories of cyclic universes?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some cosmologists propose that the Vedic concept of cosmic cycles (yugas, kalpas) may correspond to cyclic cosmological models (ekpyrotic universe, cyclic cosmology). This remains a speculative analogy.

## Canonical Sources

- Bhagavad Gītā 11.32 (Kṛṣṇa as Kāla)
- Atharvaveda 19.53-54 (Kāla Sūkta — hymn to time)
- Vaiśeṣika Sūtras 2.2.6 (Kāla as a substance)
- Arthaśāstra 1.19 (Kāla in governance)

# Shakti

## Canonical Name

Shakti

## Sanskrit

शक्ति

## Transliteration

Śakti

## Śabda

शक्ति

## Dhātu

शक् (Śak) — To be able, to have power, to be capable.

## Vyākaraṇa

Śakti is a feminine noun, i-stem declension. Derived from the root śak (to be able) with the suffix -ti. The feminine gender is significant — power in the Indian tradition is inherently feminine.

## Nirukta

"Śaknoti iti śaktiḥ" — that which is capable, that which has power. Śakti is both the power itself and the Goddess who embodies that power.

## Bīja

ह्रीं (Hrīm) — the primary bīja of Śakti. Also क्रीं (Krīm) — the bīja of Kālī-Śakti; ऐं (Aim) — the bīja of Sarasvatī-Śakti; श्रीं (Śrīm) — the bīja of Lakṣmī-Śakti.

## Tattva

Śakti-Tattva — the principle of divine power and creative energy. In Śākta philosophy: Śakti is the ultimate reality — Brahman as dynamic power. In Śaiva philosophy: Śakti is Śiva's inseparable power — "Śivaḥ śaktyā yukto yadi bhavati śaktaḥ prabhavitum" (Śiva united with Śakti is capable of creating — Soundaryalaharī 1).

## Śakti

Śakti is itself the principle of śakti — it is self-referential. The three primary śaktis: Icchā-Śakti (will-power), Jñāna-Śakti (knowledge-power), Kriyā-Śakti (action-power).

## Literal Meaning

Power; energy; capability; the Goddess; the divine feminine principle.

## Functional Meaning

Śakti is the dynamic, creative, and liberating power of the universe. It is the feminine principle that activates the masculine principle (Śiva/Puruṣa). Without Śakti, Śiva is śava (a corpse) — inert. Śakti manifests as the three primary powers: Icchā (will), Jñāna (knowledge), and Kriyā (action). In the individual, Śakti manifests as kuṇḍalinī — the dormant power at the base of the spine that, when awakened, leads to liberation.

## Ontology

In Śākta philosophy: Śakti is the ultimate reality — Brahman as dynamic power. The Goddess (Devī) is not a secondary deity but the supreme reality. In Kashmir Śaivism: Śakti is Śiva's inseparable power — the universe is Śiva-Śakti's dance. In Advaita: Śakti is Brahman's māyā-śakti — the creative power of the absolute. In Sāṃkhya: Prakṛti is the equivalent of Śakti — the primal creative power.

## Cosmology

In Śākta cosmology: the universe is the Goddess's body — she is both the creator and the creation. The Devī Māhātmya describes Śakti as the power that creates, preserves, and dissolves the universe. The concept of Śakti-pīṭhas (power seats) — 51 or 108 sacred sites where the Goddess's power is concentrated.

## Psychology

Śakti as psychological principle: the three śaktis (icchā, jñāna, kriyā) correspond to will, intellect, and action in the individual. Kuṇḍalinī-śakti is the psychological-spiritual power that, when awakened through yoga, transforms consciousness. The concept of śakti-pāta (descent of grace) — the Guru's transmission of śakti to the student.

## Governance

The concept of Śakti in governance: the ruler's power (rāja-śakti) is a manifestation of divine Śakti. The Arthaśāstra describes three types of royal power: prabhāva-śakti (power of majesty), mantra-śakti (power of counsel), utsāha-śakti (power of energy). The concept of rāṣṭra-śakti (national power) in Indian political philosophy.

## Medicine

# Prakrti

## Canonical Name

Prakrti

## Sanskrit

प्रकृति

## Transliteration

Prakṛti

## Śabda

प्रकृति

## Dhātu

प्र + कृ (Pra + Kṛ) — Pra (before, primary, forth) + Kṛ (to do, to make). The primary maker; the original nature; that which was made first.

## Vyākaraṇa

Prakṛti is a feminine noun derived from the prefix pra- and the root kṛ (to make) with the suffix -ti. The feminine gender is significant — Prakṛti is the feminine creative principle, complementary to the masculine Puruṣa.

## Nirukta

"Prakṛṣṭā kṛtiḥ prakṛtiḥ" — the primary creation. Prakṛti is the original nature from which all manifest existence emerges.

## Bīja

ह्रीं (Hrīm) — the bīja of Prakṛti as the creative power. Also क्लीं (Klīm) — the bīja of attraction and manifestation.

## Tattva

Prakṛti-Tattva — the principle of primal matter and creative nature. In Sāṃkhya: Prakṛti is one of the two ultimate realities (along with Puruṣa). It is the material cause of the universe — the primal matter from which all manifest existence evolves.

## Śakti

Prakṛti is itself the śakti — the creative power. In Śākta traditions, Prakṛti = Śakti = the Goddess. The three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas) are the three śaktis of Prakṛti.

## Literal Meaning

Nature; primal matter; the original creative principle; the feminine creative power.

## Functional Meaning

Prakṛti is the primal, undifferentiated matter from which the entire manifest universe evolves. In Sāṃkhya philosophy, Prakṛti consists of three guṇas (qualities): Sattva (clarity, luminosity), Rajas (activity, passion), Tamas (inertia, darkness). When the three guṇas are in perfect equilibrium, Prakṛti is unmanifest (avyakta). When the equilibrium is disturbed (by Puruṣa's proximity), Prakṛti begins to evolve the universe through twenty-three tattvas (principles).

## Ontology

In Sāṃkhya: Prakṛti is one of the two ultimate realities — it is the material cause of the universe. It is unconscious (acetana) but active. Puruṣa is conscious but inactive. The universe is the product of their interaction. In Advaita: Prakṛti = Māyā — the creative power of Brahman. In Viśiṣṭādvaita: Prakṛti is the body of Brahman-Viṣṇu — real and dependent on Brahman. In Śākta: Prakṛti = the Goddess — the supreme creative reality.

## Cosmology

In Sāṃkhya cosmology: from Prakṛti evolves Mahat (cosmic intellect), then Ahaṃkāra (ego-principle), then the five tanmātras (subtle elements), then the five mahābhūtas (gross elements), then the ten indriyas (sense and action organs), then manas (mind) — twenty-three tattvas in total. The universe is Prakṛti's evolution for Puruṣa's experience and eventual liberation.

## Psychology

Prakṛti as psychological principle: the three guṇas govern all psychological states. Sattva produces clarity, wisdom, and peace. Rajas produces activity, desire, and restlessness. Tamas produces inertia, delusion, and sleep. The goal of yoga is to transcend all three guṇas (triguṇātīta) and rest in Puruṣa's pure consciousness.

## Governance

The concept of Prakṛti in governance: the Arthaśāstra describes the seven elements of the state (saptāṅga) as the Prakṛti of the kingdom — king, minister, territory, fort, treasury, army, ally. The concept of rāja-prakṛti (the nature of the king) — the king's guṇa-composition determines the quality of governance.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Prakṛti is the individual's constitutional nature — the unique combination of the three doṣas (vāta, pitta, kapha) determined at conception. The concept of deha-prakṛti (body-nature) — each person has a unique Prakṛti that determines their health tendencies. Āyurvedic treatment is tailored to the individual's Prakṛti.

## Mathematics

The concept of Prakṛti in mathematics: the three guṇas as the three fundamental operations (addition/sattva, multiplication/rajas, subtraction/tamas). The concept of Prakṛti in Bījaganita (algebra) — the term prakṛti is used for the coefficient in quadratic equations.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: the three guṇas of Prakṛti are expressed in the three types of signs (movable/rajas, fixed/tamas, dual/sattva). The concept of graha-prakṛti (planetary nature) — each planet has its own guṇa composition.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: the three guṇas of Prakṛti are expressed in the three states of matter (solid/tamas, liquid/rajas, gas/sattva). The concept of dhātu-prakṛti (metal nature) — each metal has its own guṇa composition.

## Ritual

The concept of Prakṛti in ritual: the three guṇas determine the nature of ritual offerings. Sattvic offerings (milk, ghee, fruits) are for liberation. Rajasic offerings (meat, wine) are for worldly power. Tamasic offerings are for destructive purposes. The Bhagavad Gītā (17.7-10) describes the three types of food, sacrifice, and worship according to the three guṇas.

## Symbolism

The three guṇas are symbolized by three colors: white (sattva), red (rajas), black (tamas). The three strands of a rope symbolize the three guṇas — together they bind the soul. The Goddess (Devī) symbolizes Prakṛti — the creative, sustaining, and dissolving power.

- Viṣṇu (Prakṛti as his body in Viśiṣṭādvaita)

- Beyond Prakṛti is Puruṣa's realm (kaivalya)

## Related Koshas

- The Ātman (Puruṣa) is beyond Prakṛti

## Related Chakras

- The awakening of kuṇḍalinī is Prakṛti's śakti rising toward Puruṣa

## Related Yantras

- Śrī Yantra (the geometric form of Prakṛti's creative evolution)

## Related Mantras

- "Hrīm" (the bīja of Prakṛti-Śakti)
- Devī Māhātmya (the primary text of Prakṛti as the Goddess)

## Related Vidyās

- Sāṃkhya Vidyā (the science of Prakṛti and Puruṣa)
- Āyurveda (Prakṛti as individual constitution)

## Related Śāstras

- Sāṃkhya Kārikā (Īśvarakṛṣṇa) — the primary text on Prakṛti
- Bhagavad Gītā 13.19-23 (Prakṛti and Puruṣa)
- Bhagavad Gītā 14 (the three guṇas of Prakṛti)
- Caraka Saṃhitā (Prakṛti as individual constitution)

## Traditional Interpretations

- Sāṃkhya: Prakṛti is one of the two ultimate realities — the material cause of the universe
- Advaita: Prakṛti = Māyā — the creative power of Brahman
- Viśiṣṭādvaita: Prakṛti is the body of Brahman-Viṣṇu — real and dependent
- Śākta: Prakṛti = the Goddess — the supreme creative reality

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Prakṛti as the natural world
- Upaniṣadic period: Prakṛti as the creative power of Brahman
- Sāṃkhya period (pre-classical): Prakṛti systematized as the material cause
- Classical Sāṃkhya (Īśvarakṛṣṇa, ~4th century CE): Prakṛti fully systematized
- Bhagavad Gītā: Prakṛti and Puruṣa integrated into the teaching of liberation

## Cross References

- Purusha
- Maya
- Shakti
- Guna (the three qualities of Prakrti)
- Atman (Purusha — the consciousness beyond Prakrti)

## Open Research Questions

- Is the Sāṃkhya concept of Prakṛti as unconscious matter compatible with the Śākta concept of Prakṛti as conscious Goddess?
- How does the Sāṃkhya concept of Prakṛti's evolution relate to modern evolutionary biology?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some researchers propose that the Sāṃkhya concept of the three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas) corresponds to the three fundamental states of matter (plasma/gas, liquid, solid) or to the three fundamental forces of nature. This remains a speculative analogy.

## Canonical Sources

- Sāṃkhya Kārikā (Īśvarakṛṣṇa) — the primary text
- Bhagavad Gītā 13.19-23 (Prakṛti and Puruṣa)

- Caraka Saṃhitā Śārīrasthāna 1 (Prakṛti as individual constitution)

# Maya

## Canonical Name

Maya

## Sanskrit

माया

## Transliteration

Māyā

## Śabda

माया

## Dhātu

मा (Mā) — To measure, to create, to construct. Māyā is "that which measures out" or "that which creates the appearance of measure and form."

## Vyākaraṇa

Māyā is a feminine noun. Derived from the root mā (to measure/create) with the suffix -yā. In Vedic usage, māyā means "supernatural power" or "creative magic." In Advaita Vedānta, it acquires the technical meaning of "cosmic illusion."

## Nirukta

"Māyate iti māyā" — that which measures/creates. Also: "mā — not, yā — that which is" — that which is not (the appearance of what is not real). The second etymology is a later philosophical interpretation.

## Bīja

ह्रीं (Hrīm) — the bīja of Māyā-Śakti in Tantric traditions. Hrīm is the bīja of the Goddess as the creative power of illusion and liberation.

## Tattva

Māyā-Tattva — the principle of creative illusion and cosmic appearance. In Advaita: Māyā is the power of Brahman that projects the apparent multiplicity of the universe. In Kashmir Śaivism: Māyā is one of the five kañcukas (coverings) that limit the universal consciousness.

## Śakti

Māyā-Śakti — the creative and concealing power. Māyā has two functions: āvaraṇa-śakti (concealing power — it conceals Brahman) and vikṣepa-śakti (projecting power — it projects the apparent world).

## Literal Meaning

Illusion; creative power; supernatural power; the cosmic appearance.

## Functional Meaning

Māyā is the cosmic power that creates the appearance of multiplicity in the non-dual Brahman. It is neither real (sat) nor unreal (asat) — it is anirvachanīya (indescribable). Māyā operates through avidyā (ignorance) at the individual level and through the cosmic creative power at the universal level. Liberation (mokṣa) is the transcendence of māyā through jñāna (knowledge).

## Ontology

In Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Māyā is the power of Brahman that creates the appearance of the world. It is neither real nor unreal — it is mithyā (apparent). The world is not non-existent (it appears) but not ultimately real (it is not Brahman). In Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Māyā is Viṣṇu's creative power — real, not illusory. In Dvaita (Madhva): Māyā is Viṣṇu's power — the world created by māyā is real. In Kashmir Śaivism: Māyā is one of the thirty-six tattvas — a real power of Śiva that limits universal consciousness.

## Cosmology

In Purāṇic cosmology: Māyā is Viṣṇu's creative power (Yoga-Māyā) that maintains the cosmic illusion. The Devī Māhātmya describes Māyā as the Goddess herself — the cosmic creative power. In Sāṃkhya: Prakṛti (primal matter) is the equivalent of Māyā — the creative power that produces the universe for Puruṣa's experience.

## Psychology

Māyā as psychological principle: avidyā (individual ignorance) is the psychological form of cosmic māyā. The three psychological functions of māyā: āvaraṇa (concealment of the true Self), vikṣepa (projection of the false self), and mala (impurity). Liberation requires the removal of māyā through viveka (discrimination) and vairāgya (dispassion).

## Governance

The concept of māyā in governance: the ruler who is deluded by māyā governs for personal gain rather than dharma. The Arthaśāstra warns against the māyā of power — the illusion that the king is the ultimate authority. The concept of rāja-māyā (royal illusion) — the danger of rulers believing their own propaganda.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: māyā (illusion/delusion) is a cause of mental disease (mānasa-roga). The concept of prajñāparādha (crime against wisdom) — acting against one's better knowledge — is the Āyurvedic equivalent of māyā's concealing function.

## Mathematics

The concept of māyā in mathematics: the appearance of multiplicity from unity mirrors the mathematical concept of differentiation. The concept of māyā as "measurement" (from the root mā) connects to the mathematical act of measuring — imposing finite measure on the infinite.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Māyā is associated with the Moon (Candra) — the planet of illusion, reflection, and the mind. The Moon's phases represent māyā's changing appearances. The concept of graha-māyā (planetary illusion) — the apparent retrograde motion of planets is a form of māyā.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: māyā is the appearance of base metals as gold — the alchemist's task is to see through māyā to the true nature of substances. The concept of māyā in metallurgy: the surface appearance of a metal (its color, luster) may conceal its true nature.

## Ritual

The concept of māyā in ritual: ritual itself operates within māyā — it uses the apparent world to point beyond it. The concept of māyā-pūjā (worship through the apparent) — using forms, images, and rituals to transcend form. The Tantric tradition explicitly works with māyā — using the apparent world as the path to liberation.

## Symbolism

The veil symbolizes māyā — it conceals what is behind it. The mirror symbolizes māyā — it creates an apparent reflection that is not the original. The dream symbolizes māyā — vivid and real while experienced, but recognized as unreal upon waking. The magician (māyāvī) symbolizes māyā's creative power.

## Related Deities

- Devī/Mahāmāyā (the Goddess as the cosmic māyā-power)
- Viṣṇu (Yoga-Māyā — his creative power)
- Śiva (Māyā as his śakti)
- Durgā (the Goddess who wields māyā to protect dharma)

## Related Lokas

- All lokas are within māyā — they are māyā's projections
- Brahmaloka is beyond māyā

## Related Koshas

- All five koshas are māyā's projections
- Ānandamaya Kosha is the subtlest form of māyā

## Related Chakras

- Ājñā (third eye) — the chakra of discrimination that sees through māyā
- Sahasrāra (crown) — beyond māyā

## Related Yantras

- Śrī Yantra (the geometric form of Māyā-Śakti's creative power)
- Hrīm Yantra (the yantra of Māyā-bīja)

## Related Mantras

- "Hrīm" (the bīja of Māyā-Śakti)
- "Om aim hrīm klīm cāmuṇḍāyai vicce" (Navārṇa Mantra — invoking the Goddess beyond māyā)

## Related Vidyās

- Māyā Vidyā (the science of cosmic illusion — Advaita Vedānta)
- Śakti Vidyā (the science of the Goddess as māyā-power)

## Related Śāstras

- Māṇḍūkya Kārikā (Gauḍapāda — māyā as the basis of the apparent world)
- Vivekacūḍāmaṇi (Śaṅkara — māyā and its transcendence)
- Devī Māhātmya (Māyā as the Goddess)
- Yoga Vāsiṣṭha (māyā and liberation)

## Traditional Interpretations

- Advaita Vedānta: Māyā is the cosmic illusion — neither real nor unreal; transcended by jñāna
- Viśiṣṭādvaita: Māyā is Viṣṇu's real creative power — the world is real
- Dvaita: Māyā is Viṣṇu's power — the world created by māyā is real
- Śākta: Māyā is the Goddess herself — the creative power of the universe
- Kashmir Śaivism: Māyā is one of the thirty-six tattvas — a real power of Śiva

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Māyā as supernatural creative power (of Varuṇa, Indra)
- Upaniṣadic period: Māyā as the creative power of Brahman
- Gauḍapāda (7th century CE): Māyā as the basis of the apparent world
- Śaṅkara (8th century CE): Māyā as cosmic illusion — the central concept of Advaita
- Rāmānuja (11th century CE): Critique of Śaṅkara's māyā — the world is real
- Modern: Māyā as a concept in comparative philosophy and consciousness studies

## Cross References

- Brahman
- Avidya (ignorance — individual māyā)
- Prakrti (Sāṃkhya equivalent)
- Shakti
- Moksha (liberation from māyā)

## Open Research Questions

- Is Śaṅkara's concept of māyā coherent? Can something be "neither real nor unreal"?
- How does the Advaita concept of māyā relate to the Buddhist concept of śūnyatā (emptiness)?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some philosophers of mind propose that the Advaita concept of māyā anticipates the modern philosophical problem of the "veil of perception" — the question of whether we perceive reality directly or only its appearances. This remains a philosophical analogy.

## Canonical Sources

- Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10 (māyā as the Goddess's creative power)
- Māṇḍūkya Kārikā (Gauḍapāda)
- Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya (Śaṅkara)
- Devī Māhātmya 1.55-56 (Mahāmāyā)
- Bhagavad Gītā 7.14 (daivī māyā — divine illusion)

# Brahman

## Canonical Name

Brahman

## Sanskrit

ब्रह्मन्

## Transliteration

Brahman

## Śabda

ब्रह्मन्

## Dhātu

बृह् (Bṛh) — To expand, to grow, to be great.

## Vyākaraṇa

Brahman is a neuter noun (not to be confused with Brahmā, the masculine creator deity, or Brāhmaṇa, the priestly class). Derived from the root bṛh with the suffix -man. The neuter gender indicates that Brahman transcends all categories including gender.

## Nirukta

Yāska: "bṛhati iti brahma" — that which is great, that which expands. Brahman is the infinitely expanding reality that underlies all existence.

## Bīja

ॐ (Om/Auṃ) — the primordial sound that is the sonic form of Brahman. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad opens: "Auṃ ity etad akṣaram idaṃ sarvam" — Om, this syllable is all this.

## Tattva

Brahma-Tattva — the principle of absolute, infinite, self-luminous reality. Brahman is described as Sat-Cit-Ānanda (Being-Consciousness-Bliss) — not three qualities but three aspects of one indivisible reality.

## Śakti

Brahman's śakti is Māyā — the creative power that projects the apparent multiplicity of the universe. In Śākta traditions, Brahman without Śakti is inert (śava); Brahman with Śakti is Śiva (the living absolute).

## Literal Meaning

The Absolute; the Infinite; the Ultimate Reality; the Ground of Being.

## Functional Meaning

Brahman is the infinite, eternal, unchanging absolute reality that is the ground of all existence. It is both the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) and the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa) of the universe. Brahman is described via two approaches: Nirguṇa Brahman (without attributes — the absolute beyond all description) and Saguṇa Brahman (with attributes — the personal God, Īśvara). The Upaniṣads teach that Brahman is identical with Ātman (the individual Self).

## Ontology

In Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Brahman alone is real (Brahma satyam); the world is appearance (jagat mithyā); the individual self is Brahman (jīvo brahmaiva nāparaḥ). In Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Brahman is real, personal (Viṣṇu), and the universe and souls are Brahman's body. In Dvaita (Madhva): Brahman (Viṣṇu) is real and eternally distinct from souls and world. In Śaiva Siddhānta: Brahman is Śiva, the supreme reality with infinite śaktis.

## Cosmology

Brahman is the source, sustainer, and dissolution point of all universes. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad: "yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante" — from which all beings are born, by which they live, into which they return — that is Brahman. The Purāṇas describe Brahman as the ocean from which the universe arises like waves. The concept of Brahmaṇḍa (Brahman's egg) is the cosmic egg from which the universe hatches.

## Psychology

Brahman as psychological reality: the deepest layer of consciousness is Brahman. In Yoga psychology, the state of samādhi (absorption) is the direct experience of Brahman. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad identifies Brahman with the fourth state of consciousness (turīya) that underlies waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. The experience of Brahman is described as "neti neti" (not this, not this) — Brahman cannot be grasped by the mind but is the ground of the mind.

## Governance

The concept of Brahman in governance: the ideal ruler is one who has realized Brahman and governs from that realization. The Arthaśāstra's concept of the philosopher-king parallels the Upaniṣadic ideal of the Brahman-realized ruler. The concept of Brahma-rāṣṭra (the kingdom of Brahman) appears in Vedic literature as the ideal polity.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Brahman is the ultimate source of health (ārogya). The concept of Brahma-cakra (the cycle of Brahman) underlies the Āyurvedic understanding of the body as a microcosm of the universe. The highest healing is Brahma-jñāna (knowledge of Brahman) which removes the root cause of all disease — avidyā (ignorance).

## Mathematics

The concept of Brahman in mathematics: Brahman as the infinite (ananta) is the philosophical basis for the Indian mathematical concept of infinity. The concept of śūnya (zero) as the void from which all numbers emerge mirrors the Brahman-as-source concept. The Upaniṣadic statement "pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam" (that is full, this is full) is a mathematical statement about the nature of infinity.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Brahman is identified with the cosmic space (ākāśa) in which all celestial bodies move. The concept of Brahma-muhūrta (the hour of Brahman — 1.5 hours before sunrise) is the most auspicious time for spiritual practice. The Milky Way (Ākāśagaṅgā) is considered the visible form of Brahman's cosmic body.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: Brahman is the philosophical gold (parama-suvarṇa) — the ultimate substance that all metals aspire to become. The alchemical process of transmutation mirrors the spiritual process of realizing Brahman beneath the apparent multiplicity of substances.

## Ritual

The Brahma-yajña (sacrifice to Brahman) is the daily recitation of the Vedas — the highest ritual act. The Upanayana ceremony initiates the student into the study of Brahman. The Mahāvākyas are transmitted in ritual contexts as the direct teaching of Brahman. The concept of Brahma-vidyā (knowledge of Brahman) is the ultimate goal of all Vedic ritual.

## Symbolism

Om (ॐ) is the primary symbol of Brahman — the sound of the universe. The infinite space (ākāśa) symbolizes Brahman's all-pervading nature. The ocean symbolizes Brahman — waves (individual beings) arise from and return to the ocean. The sun symbolizes Nirguṇa Brahman — self-luminous, the source of all light. The bindu (point) in the center of a yantra represents Brahman as the source of all manifestation.

## Related Deities

- Brahman is not a deity but the ground of all deities

- Viṣṇu (the preserver) is Saguṇa Brahman's sustaining aspect
- Śiva (the destroyer) is Saguṇa Brahman's dissolving aspect
- Devī (the Goddess) is Brahman's Śakti — the dynamic aspect of the absolute

# Kala

## Canonical Name

Kala

## Sanskrit

काल

## Transliteration

Kāla

## Śabda

काल

## Dhātu

कल् (Kal) — To count, to calculate; also connected to कल् (Kal) — to drive, to impel. Time is that which counts/measures and that which drives all things forward.

## Vyākaraṇa

Kāla is a masculine noun. It has two distinct meanings: (1) time (the cosmic principle), (2) death/Yama (the lord of time). The same word means both "time" and "death" — time is the force that leads all things to death.

## Nirukta

"Kalayati iti kālaḥ" — that which counts/measures. Also: "kālayati sarvam iti kālaḥ" — that which drives everything forward. Time is the universal driver.

## Bīja

क्रीं (Krīm) — the bīja of Kālī (the Goddess of time and death). Also कं (Kaṃ) — the bīja of Brahmā (the creator who operates within time).

## Tattva

Kāla-Tattva — the principle of time. In Sāṃkhya: Kāla is not a separate tattva but the mode of Prakṛti's activity. In Kashmir Śaivism: Kāla is one of the five kañcukas (coverings) that limit the universal consciousness — it limits the soul's experience to a particular time.

## Śakti

Kāla-Śakti — the power of time. The śakti that drives all change and transformation. Kālī (the Goddess of time) is the personification of Kāla-Śakti.

## Literal Meaning

Time; the right time; death; the black one (Kāla = black = death).

## Functional Meaning

Kāla is the universal principle of time that governs all change, growth, decay, and death. It operates at multiple levels: Kṣaṇa (moment), Muhūrta (48 minutes), Ahorātra (day-night), Pakṣa (fortnight), Māsa (month), Ṛtu (season), Ayana (half-year), Saṃvatsara (year), Yuga (cosmic age), Kalpa (cosmic cycle). The Bhagavad Gītā (11.32) identifies Kāla with Kṛṣṇa himself: "Kālo'smi loka-kṣaya-kṛt pravṛddhaḥ" — I am time, the destroyer of worlds.

## Ontology

In Vaiśeṣika: Kāla is one of the nine dravyas (substances) — eternal, all-pervading, the cause of all temporal relations. In Sāṃkhya: Kāla is not a separate substance but the mode of Prakṛti's activity. In Advaita: Kāla is within māyā — from the absolute standpoint, there is no time. In Kashmir Śaivism: Kāla is one of the five kañcukas that limit the soul.

## Cosmology

In Vedic cosmology: the four yugas (Kṛta/Satya, Tretā, Dvāpara, Kali) constitute a mahāyuga (4,320,000 years). 1000 mahāyugas = one kalpa (day of Brahmā = 4.32 billion years). The concept of mahāpralaya (great dissolution) at the end of Brahmā's life (311 trillion years). The Purāṇas describe Kāla as the cosmic force that drives the universe through its cycles.

## Psychology

Kāla as psychological principle: the experience of time is subjective — time flies in joy and drags in suffering. The concept of kāla-jñāna (knowledge of time) — the wise person knows the right time for action. The concept of kāla-yoga (the yoga of time) — acting in alignment with the cosmic time.

## Governance

The concept of Kāla in governance: the Arthaśāstra emphasizes kāla (timing) as one of the most important factors in governance. The concept of kāla-nīti (time-policy) — the right action at the right time. The concept of kāla-cakra (wheel of time) in political philosophy — empires rise and fall according to the wheel of time.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Kāla (time) is one of the three causes of disease (along with karma and prajñāparādha). The concept of kāla-parīkṣā (examination of time) — the physician must consider the time of day, season, and stage of life in diagnosis and treatment. The concept of kāla-bala (strength of time) — certain times are more favorable for treatment.

## Mathematics

In Vedic mathematics: Kāla is the basis of the Indian number system — the large numbers (millions, billions, trillions) were developed to measure cosmic time. The concept of kāla-gaṇita (time calculation) — the mathematics of astronomical cycles.

## Astronomy

Jyotiṣa (Vedic astronomy) is fundamentally the science of Kāla — tracking the movements of celestial bodies to determine auspicious times. The concept of kāla-cakra (wheel of time) in Jyotiṣa — the zodiac as the wheel of cosmic time. The nakṣatra system, the tithi (lunar day), and the muhūrta (auspicious time) are all expressions of Kāla.

## Metallurgy

The concept of Kāla in metallurgy: the right time for metallurgical processes — certain times are more auspicious for smelting, forging, and casting. The concept of kāla-karma (time-action) in metallurgy.

## Ritual

The concept of Kāla in ritual: all Vedic rituals are performed at specific times determined by Jyotiṣa. The concept of muhūrta (auspicious time) — the right moment for ritual action. The concept of kāla-pūjā (worship of time) — the Kālī pūjā is the worship of the Goddess of time.

## Symbolism

The wheel (cakra) symbolizes Kāla — the wheel of time that turns without stopping. The serpent eating its own tail (Ouroboros) symbolizes the cyclical nature of time. The skull (kapāla) symbolizes Kāla as death. The hourglass symbolizes the finite nature of human time within infinite cosmic time.

# Prakrti

## Canonical Name

Prakrti

## Sanskrit

प्रकृति

## Transliteration

Prakṛti

## Śabda

प्रकृति

## Dhātu

प्र + कृ (Pra + Kṛ) — Pra (before, primary, forth) + Kṛ (to do, to make). The primary maker; the original nature; that which was made first.

## Vyākaraṇa

Prakṛti is a feminine noun derived from the prefix pra- and the root kṛ (to make) with the suffix -ti. The feminine gender is significant — Prakṛti is the feminine creative principle, complementary to the masculine Puruṣa.

## Nirukta

"Prakṛṣṭā kṛtiḥ prakṛtiḥ" — the primary creation. Prakṛti is the original nature from which all manifest existence emerges.

## Bīja

ह्रीं (Hrīm) — the bīja of Prakṛti as the creative power. Also क्लीं (Klīm) — the bīja of attraction and manifestation.

## Tattva

Prakṛti-Tattva — the principle of primal matter and creative nature. In Sāṃkhya: Prakṛti is one of the two ultimate realities (along with Puruṣa). It is the material cause of the universe — the primal matter from which all manifest existence evolves.

## Śakti

Prakṛti is itself the śakti — the creative power. In Śākta traditions, Prakṛti = Śakti = the Goddess. The three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas) are the three śaktis of Prakṛti.

## Literal Meaning

Nature; primal matter; the original creative principle; the feminine creative power.

## Functional Meaning

Prakṛti is the primal, undifferentiated matter from which the entire manifest universe evolves. In Sāṃkhya philosophy, Prakṛti consists of three guṇas (qualities): Sattva (clarity, luminosity), Rajas (activity, passion), Tamas (inertia, darkness). When the three guṇas are in perfect equilibrium, Prakṛti is unmanifest (avyakta). When the equilibrium is disturbed (by Puruṣa's proximity), Prakṛti begins to evolve the universe through twenty-three tattvas (principles).

## Ontology

In Sāṃkhya: Prakṛti is one of the two ultimate realities — it is the material cause of the universe. It is unconscious (acetana) but active. Puruṣa is conscious but inactive. The universe is the product of their interaction. In Advaita: Prakṛti = Māyā — the creative power of Brahman. In Viśiṣṭādvaita: Prakṛti is the body of Brahman-Viṣṇu — real and dependent on Brahman. In Śākta: Prakṛti = the Goddess — the supreme creative reality.

## Cosmology

In Sāṃkhya cosmology: from Prakṛti evolves Mahat (cosmic intellect), then Ahaṃkāra (ego-principle), then the five tanmātras (subtle elements), then the five mahābhūtas (gross elements), then the ten indriyas (sense and action organs), then manas (mind) — twenty-three tattvas in total. The universe is Prakṛti's evolution for Puruṣa's experience and eventual liberation.

## Psychology

Prakṛti as psychological principle: the three guṇas govern all psychological states. Sattva produces clarity, wisdom, and peace. Rajas produces activity, desire, and restlessness. Tamas produces inertia, delusion, and sleep. The goal of yoga is to transcend all three guṇas (triguṇātīta) and rest in Puruṣa's pure consciousness.

## Governance

The concept of Prakṛti in governance: the Arthaśāstra describes the seven elements of the state (saptāṅga) as the Prakṛti of the kingdom — king, minister, territory, fort, treasury, army, ally. The concept of rāja-prakṛti (the nature of the king) — the king's guṇa-composition determines the quality of governance.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Prakṛti is the individual's constitutional nature — the unique combination of the three doṣas (vāta, pitta, kapha) determined at conception. The concept of deha-prakṛti (body-nature) — each person has a unique Prakṛti that determines their health tendencies. Āyurvedic treatment is tailored to the individual's Prakṛti.

## Mathematics

The concept of Prakṛti in mathematics: the three guṇas as the three fundamental operations (addition/sattva, multiplication/rajas, subtraction/tamas). The concept of Prakṛti in Bījaganita (algebra) — the term prakṛti is used for the coefficient in quadratic equations.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: the three guṇas of Prakṛti are expressed in the three types of signs (movable/rajas, fixed/tamas, dual/sattva). The concept of graha-prakṛti (planetary nature) — each planet has its own guṇa composition.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: the three guṇas of Prakṛti are expressed in the three states of matter (solid/tamas, liquid/rajas, gas/sattva). The concept of dhātu-prakṛti (metal nature) — each metal has its own guṇa composition.

## Ritual

The concept of Prakṛti in ritual: the three guṇas determine the nature of ritual offerings. Sattvic offerings (milk, ghee, fruits) are for liberation. Rajasic offerings (meat, wine) are for worldly power. Tamasic offerings are for destructive purposes. The Bhagavad Gītā (17.7-10) describes the three types of food, sacrifice, and worship according to the three guṇas.

## Symbolism

The three guṇas are symbolized by three colors: white (sattva), red (rajas), black (tamas). The three strands of a rope symbolize the three guṇas — together they bind the soul. The Goddess (Devī) symbolizes Prakṛti — the creative, sustaining, and dissolving power.

# Shakti

## Canonical Name

Shakti

## Sanskrit

शक्ति

## Transliteration

Śakti

## Śabda

शक्ति

## Dhātu

शक् (Śak) — To be able, to have power, to be capable.

## Vyākaraṇa

Śakti is a feminine noun, i-stem declension. Derived from the root śak (to be able) with the suffix -ti. The feminine gender is significant — power in the Indian tradition is inherently feminine.

## Nirukta

"Śaknoti iti śaktiḥ" — that which is capable, that which has power. Śakti is both the power itself and the Goddess who embodies that power.

## Bīja

ह्रीं (Hrīm) — the primary bīja of Śakti. Also क्रीं (Krīm) — the bīja of Kālī-Śakti; ऐं (Aim) — the bīja of Sarasvatī-Śakti; श्रीं (Śrīm) — the bīja of Lakṣmī-Śakti.

## Tattva

Śakti-Tattva — the principle of divine power and creative energy. In Śākta philosophy: Śakti is the ultimate reality — Brahman as dynamic power. In Śaiva philosophy: Śakti is Śiva's inseparable power — "Śivaḥ śaktyā yukto yadi bhavati śaktaḥ prabhavitum" (Śiva united with Śakti is capable of creating — Soundaryalaharī 1).

## Śakti

Śakti is itself the principle of śakti — it is self-referential. The three primary śaktis: Icchā-Śakti (will-power), Jñāna-Śakti (knowledge-power), Kriyā-Śakti (action-power).

## Literal Meaning

Power; energy; capability; the Goddess; the divine feminine principle.

## Functional Meaning

Śakti is the dynamic, creative, and liberating power of the universe. It is the feminine principle that activates the masculine principle (Śiva/Puruṣa). Without Śakti, Śiva is śava (a corpse) — inert. Śakti manifests as the three primary powers: Icchā (will), Jñāna (knowledge), and Kriyā (action). In the individual, Śakti manifests as kuṇḍalinī — the dormant power at the base of the spine that, when awakened, leads to liberation.

## Ontology

In Śākta philosophy: Śakti is the ultimate reality — Brahman as dynamic power. The Goddess (Devī) is not a secondary deity but the supreme reality. In Kashmir Śaivism: Śakti is Śiva's inseparable power — the universe is Śiva-Śakti's dance. In Advaita: Śakti is Brahman's māyā-śakti — the creative power of the absolute. In Sāṃkhya: Prakṛti is the equivalent of Śakti — the primal creative power.

## Cosmology

In Śākta cosmology: the universe is the Goddess's body — she is both the creator and the creation. The Devī Māhātmya describes Śakti as the power that creates, preserves, and dissolves the universe. The concept of Śakti-pīṭhas (power seats) — 51 or 108 sacred sites where the Goddess's power is concentrated.

## Psychology

Śakti as psychological principle: the three śaktis (icchā, jñāna, kriyā) correspond to will, intellect, and action in the individual. Kuṇḍalinī-śakti is the psychological-spiritual power that, when awakened through yoga, transforms consciousness. The concept of śakti-pāta (descent of grace) — the Guru's transmission of śakti to the student.

## Governance

The concept of Śakti in governance: the ruler's power (rāja-śakti) is a manifestation of divine Śakti. The Arthaśāstra describes three types of royal power: prabhāva-śakti (power of majesty), mantra-śakti (power of counsel), utsāha-śakti (power of energy). The concept of rāṣṭra-śakti (national power) in Indian political philosophy.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Śakti is the vital power (ojas) — the refined essence of all bodily tissues. The concept of śakti in Āyurvedic therapy: building ojas (vital power) through proper diet, lifestyle, and herbs. The concept of śakti-vardhana (power enhancement) in Āyurvedic medicine.

## Mathematics

The concept of Śakti in mathematics: the power function (śakti) in Indian mathematics — the concept of raising a number to a power. The Bījaganita (algebra) of Bhāskara uses śakti in the sense of "square" (the power of a number).

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Śakti is associated with the Moon (Candra) and Venus (Śukra) — the feminine planets. The concept of graha-śakti (planetary power) — each planet has its own śakti. The nakṣatra Śakti is associated with specific astrological powers.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: Śakti is the feminine principle in alchemy — sulfur (gandhaka) is the Śakti to mercury's (pārada) Śiva. The union of mercury and sulfur is the alchemical Śiva-Śakti union. The concept of dhātu-śakti (power of metals) — each metal has its own śakti.

## Ritual

The Śakti-pūjā (worship of the Goddess) is the primary Śākta ritual. The Navārātra (nine nights of the Goddess) is the primary Śākta festival. The concept of śakti-upāsanā (worship of power) — using the Goddess's power for liberation. The Tantric ritual of śakti-sādhana (practice with the Goddess's power).

## Symbolism

The triangle (trikona) pointing downward symbolizes Śakti — the feminine, receptive, creative power. The lotus symbolizes Śakti's creative power — blooming from the waters of consciousness. The lion (siṃha) is Śakti's vehicle — representing her power over the ego. The trident (triśūla) represents Śakti's three powers (icchā, jñāna, kriyā).

# Maya

## Canonical Name

Maya

## Sanskrit

माया

## Transliteration

Māyā

## Śabda

माया

## Dhātu

मा (Mā) — To measure, to create, to construct. Māyā is "that which measures out" or "that which creates the appearance of measure and form."

## Vyākaraṇa

Māyā is a feminine noun. Derived from the root mā (to measure/create) with the suffix -yā. In Vedic usage, māyā means "supernatural power" or "creative magic." In Advaita Vedānta, it acquires the technical meaning of "cosmic illusion."

## Nirukta

"Māyate iti māyā" — that which measures/creates. Also: "mā — not, yā — that which is" — that which is not (the appearance of what is not real). The second etymology is a later philosophical interpretation.

## Bīja

ह्रीं (Hrīm) — the bīja of Māyā-Śakti in Tantric traditions. Hrīm is the bīja of the Goddess as the creative power of illusion and liberation.

## Tattva

Māyā-Tattva — the principle of creative illusion and cosmic appearance. In Advaita: Māyā is the power of Brahman that projects the apparent multiplicity of the universe. In Kashmir Śaivism: Māyā is one of the five kañcukas (coverings) that limit the universal consciousness.

## Śakti

Māyā-Śakti — the creative and concealing power. Māyā has two functions: āvaraṇa-śakti (concealing power — it conceals Brahman) and vikṣepa-śakti (projecting power — it projects the apparent world).

## Literal Meaning

Illusion; creative power; supernatural power; the cosmic appearance.

## Functional Meaning

Māyā is the cosmic power that creates the appearance of multiplicity in the non-dual Brahman. It is neither real (sat) nor unreal (asat) — it is anirvachanīya (indescribable). Māyā operates through avidyā (ignorance) at the individual level and through the cosmic creative power at the universal level. Liberation (mokṣa) is the transcendence of māyā through jñāna (knowledge).

## Ontology

In Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Māyā is the power of Brahman that creates the appearance of the world. It is neither real nor unreal — it is mithyā (apparent). The world is not non-existent (it appears) but not ultimately real (it is not Brahman). In Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Māyā is Viṣṇu's creative power — real, not illusory. In Dvaita (Madhva): Māyā is Viṣṇu's power — the world created by māyā is real. In Kashmir Śaivism: Māyā is one of the thirty-six tattvas — a real power of Śiva that limits universal consciousness.

## Cosmology

In Purāṇic cosmology: Māyā is Viṣṇu's creative power (Yoga-Māyā) that maintains the cosmic illusion. The Devī Māhātmya describes Māyā as the Goddess herself — the cosmic creative power. In Sāṃkhya: Prakṛti (primal matter) is the equivalent of Māyā — the creative power that produces the universe for Puruṣa's experience.

## Psychology

Māyā as psychological principle: avidyā (individual ignorance) is the psychological form of cosmic māyā. The three psychological functions of māyā: āvaraṇa (concealment of the true Self), vikṣepa (projection of the false self), and mala (impurity). Liberation requires the removal of māyā through viveka (discrimination) and vairāgya (dispassion).

## Governance

The concept of māyā in governance: the ruler who is deluded by māyā governs for personal gain rather than dharma. The Arthaśāstra warns against the māyā of power — the illusion that the king is the ultimate authority. The concept of rāja-māyā (royal illusion) — the danger of rulers believing their own propaganda.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: māyā (illusion/delusion) is a cause of mental disease (mānasa-roga). The concept of prajñāparādha (crime against wisdom) — acting against one's better knowledge — is the Āyurvedic equivalent of māyā's concealing function.

## Mathematics

The concept of māyā in mathematics: the appearance of multiplicity from unity mirrors the mathematical concept of differentiation. The concept of māyā as "measurement" (from the root mā) connects to the mathematical act of measuring — imposing finite measure on the infinite.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Māyā is associated with the Moon (Candra) — the planet of illusion, reflection, and the mind. The Moon's phases represent māyā's changing appearances. The concept of graha-māyā (planetary illusion) — the apparent retrograde motion of planets is a form of māyā.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: māyā is the appearance of base metals as gold — the alchemist's task is to see through māyā to the true nature of substances. The concept of māyā in metallurgy: the surface appearance of a metal (its color, luster) may conceal its true nature.

## Ritual

The concept of māyā in ritual: ritual itself operates within māyā — it uses the apparent world to point beyond it. The concept of māyā-pūjā (worship through the apparent) — using forms, images, and rituals to transcend form. The Tantric tradition explicitly works with māyā — using the apparent world as the path to liberation.

## Symbolism

The veil symbolizes māyā — it conceals what is behind it. The mirror symbolizes māyā — it creates an apparent reflection that is not the original. The dream symbolizes māyā — vivid and real while experienced, but recognized as unreal upon waking. The magician (māyāvī) symbolizes māyā's creative power.

## Related Deities

- Devī/Mahāmāyā (the Goddess as the cosmic māyā-power)
- Viṣṇu (Yoga-Māyā — his creative power)
- Śiva (Māyā as his śakti)
- Durgā (the Goddess who wields māyā to protect dharma)

## Related Lokas

- All lokas are within māyā — they are māyā's projections
- Brahmaloka is beyond māyā

## Related Koshas

- All five koshas are māyā's projections
- Ānandamaya Kosha is the subtlest form of māyā

## Related Chakras

- Ājñā (third eye) — the chakra of discrimination that sees through māyā
- Sahasrāra (crown) — beyond māyā

## Related Yantras

- Śrī Yantra (the geometric form of Māyā-Śakti's creative power)
- Hrīm Yantra (the yantra of Māyā-bīja)

## Related Mantras

- "Hrīm" (the bīja of Māyā-Śakti)
- "Om aim hrīm klīm cāmuṇḍāyai vicce" (Navārṇa Mantra — invoking the Goddess beyond māyā)

## Related Vidyās

- Māyā Vidyā (the science of cosmic illusion — Advaita Vedānta)
- Śakti Vidyā (the science of the Goddess as māyā-power)

## Related Śāstras

- Māṇḍūkya Kārikā (Gauḍapāda — māyā as the basis of the apparent world)
- Vivekacūḍāmaṇi (Śaṅkara — māyā and its transcendence)
- Devī Māhātmya (Māyā as the Goddess)
- Yoga Vāsiṣṭha (māyā and liberation)

## Traditional Interpretations

- Advaita Vedānta: Māyā is the cosmic illusion — neither real nor unreal; transcended by jñāna
- Viśiṣṭādvaita: Māyā is Viṣṇu's real creative power — the world is real
- Dvaita: Māyā is Viṣṇu's power — the world created by māyā is real
- Śākta: Māyā is the Goddess herself — the creative power of the universe
- Kashmir Śaivism: Māyā is one of the thirty-six tattvas — a real power of Śiva

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Māyā as supernatural creative power (of Varuṇa, Indra)
- Upaniṣadic period: Māyā as the creative power of Brahman
- Gauḍapāda (7th century CE): Māyā as the basis of the apparent world
- Śaṅkara (8th century CE): Māyā as cosmic illusion — the central concept of Advaita
- Rāmānuja (11th century CE): Critique of Śaṅkara's māyā — the world is real
- Modern: Māyā as a concept in comparative philosophy and consciousness studies

## Cross References

- Brahman
- Avidya (ignorance — individual māyā)
- Prakrti (Sāṃkhya equivalent)
- Shakti
- Moksha (liberation from māyā)

## Open Research Questions

- Is Śaṅkara's concept of māyā coherent? Can something be "neither real nor unreal"?
- How does the Advaita concept of māyā relate to the Buddhist concept of śūnyatā (emptiness)?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some philosophers of mind propose that the Advaita concept of māyā anticipates the modern philosophical problem of the "veil of perception" — the question of whether we perceive reality directly or only its appearances. This remains a philosophical analogy.

## Canonical Sources

- Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10 (māyā as the Goddess's creative power)
- Māṇḍūkya Kārikā (Gauḍapāda)
- Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya (Śaṅkara)
- Devī Māhātmya 1.55-56 (Mahāmāyā)
- Bhagavad Gītā 7.14 (daivī māyā — divine illusion)
